item.research_question: What are the time–temperature-dependent oxidation mechanisms and phase transformations of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy in vacuum and air environments, and how do they compare with thermodynamic predictions?
item.material_system: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (20 at.% each of Cr, Co, Fe, Mn, Ni)
item.processing_route: Arc melting and drop casting of 3 N purity elements in a vacuum of ~7 × 10⁻⁴ Pa followed by argon refilling to ~8.4 × 10⁴ Pa; annealing at 900 °C for 48 h; cold rolling to 1.6 mm thickness; mechanical and mirror polishing with 1 μm diamond suspension for in situ analysis
item.test_conditions: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) from 25 °C to 1100 °C at 15 °C/min heating rate with 5 min stabilization at 50 °C intervals; two environments: vacuum (~4.2 × 10⁻⁶ atm) and air (1.0 atm); CuKα radiation (λ = 0.154 nm), 40 kV, 40 mA, 2θ range 30–80°
key_findings: Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air, leading to non-protective oxides and bulk Mn depletion.
In vacuum, only MnO (halite-type) formed at 700 °C, with no Cr₂O₃, Fe₂O₃, or Fe₃O₄ detected.
In air, Mn₂O₃ formed initially at 550 °C, transforming to Mn₃O₄ at 950 °C, with MnCr₂O₄ appearing at 800 °C.
No protective Cr₂O₃ layer formed in either environment; instead, mixed oxides (Mn₃O₄, MnCr₂O₄, Fe₃Mn₃O₈) dominated.
ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxides in vacuum and air, but experiments showed halite (MnO) in vacuum and mixed spinels in air.
Oxide scale thickness in air reached 1.58–3.45 μm, while in vacuum it was <0.5 μm.
Mn diffusion rate is two orders of magnitude faster than Cr, resulting in Mn-rich outer oxide layers.
item.mechanism: Mn preferentially diffuses outward due to its high vapor pressure and fast diffusion rate, reacting with available oxygen to form non-protective oxides (MnO in vacuum, Mn₂O₃/Mn₃O₄ in air). The absence of a protective Cr₂O₃ barrier allows continued Mn oxidation and depletion. Mixed oxides form due to concurrent diffusion of Cr and Fe, but binary Cr/Fe oxides do not fully develop within the experimental timeframe.
item.limitations: Thermodynamic calculations assume equilibrium conditions and do not account for kinetic effects such as diffusion, nucleation, and surface reactions. The study's timescale may be insufficient for stable binary oxides of Cr and Fe to fully form. Discrepancies between ThermoCalc predictions and experimental results may arise from kinetic limitations and database accuracy at high temperatures.
item.future_work: Future research should integrate thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential thermal analysis (DTA), as well as in situ microscopy or spectroscopy, to better understand oxidation kinetics and real-time oxide layer evolution.
quotes: Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn
no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi
ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results
